title: My AI game dev workflow: 100% AI prototype, ~30% AI by the demo, and I still own the engine
author: WritingDecent9543
selftext:
Here's the workflow I use, from idea to demo:



1. One idea + a rough system sketch.

2. All-in AI prototype: docs, art, music and code are 100% AI.

3. Polish the prototype: cut what isn't fun or isn't needed, add elements with orthogonal design. Still 100% AI, but this stage outputs the inputs for the next one: a demo plan, prototype Aseprite files, audio + interactive music rules, and all text as i18n CSV/JSON.

4. Human polish, following the plan: hand-polished Aseprite art, sound and interactive music. Art and audio drop to \~30% AI. Translation goes to a third-party vendor at \~70% AI (AI handles the basics and UI text well, but a human review is still worth it).

5. Code stays 100% AI, but the engine, architecture and project structure underneath are designed by me. That foundation is what makes it work. If you're proud of hand-writing business code, why not write your own OS first?



The full release is just another loop of the same process with new content.



Curious how others split it: what's your AI % per discipline right now, and where do you pull humans back in?

comments.author: thecrownforge
comments.body: for code, the percentage tells me less than what gets checked before release. do you run a full playthrough on top of the unit and logic tests? bugs often sit where two systems meet, even when each one passes on its own

replies.author: WritingDecent9543
replies.body:
Yes, I play through the whole game myself many, many times. That’s an essential part of my job as the designer, beyond just checking for bugs.

In my case, I’ve spent a lot of time refining the underlying systems: quests, saves, variables, dialogue, inventory, animation, particles, etc. Those form the foundation of my games, and games built on top of them have been very stable in practice. From memory, I’ve encountered fewer than five system or game logic bugs over the past six months, excluding visual issues like overlapping UI or poor layouts.

Unit tests and automated headless tests run by AI are a given in my workflow. I also have AI agents play through the entire game at different difficulty levels to verify that every section can be completed on each build.

So yes, full playthroughs are absolutely part of the process, both automated and manual.
